books.section: Topic 4.2 The Rise of Political Parties and the Era of Jefferson, C. The Louisiana Purchase and Territorial Expansion
The Louisiana Purchase and the Lewis and Clark Expedition

stimulus.source_note: Charles M. Russell, Lewis and Clark Meeting Indians at Ross' Hole, September 4, 1805, mural painted 1912, public domain (artist died 1926). A later depiction, not a record made on the expedition.
stimulus.text: Charles M. Russell's 1912 mural of Lewis and Clark meeting Native peoples at Ross' Hole, September 4, 1805: mounted Native riders approach the expedition party on the right, with tipis, mountains, and clouds behind them. The mural was painted more than a century after the meeting it shows.

source: original; stimulus image from the shared pool, Charles M. Russell's 1912 mural of the Ross' Hole meeting
stem: The expedition shown in the image was sent west by Jefferson mainly to

options.text: conquer Mexico and claim its silver mines for the United States
options.misconception: The expedition headed northwest to the Pacific, not south into Mexico, and it was a party of explorers, not an army.

options.text: build forts to keep British traders out of the Louisiana Territory
options.misconception: The party was too small to hold forts, and its orders were to explore and report, not to garrison the territory.

options.text: find gold in the Rocky Mountains
options.misconception: The expedition sought routes, knowledge, and trade contacts, not gold; no gold rush followed it.

options.text: explore and map the new territory and report on what it held

rationales.A: The expedition headed northwest to the Pacific, not south into Mexico, and it was a party of explorers, not an army.
rationales.B: The party was too small to hold forts, and its orders were to explore and report, not to garrison the territory.
rationales.C: The expedition sought routes, knowledge, and trade contacts, not gold. No gold rush followed it.
rationales.D: Lewis and Clark left for the Pacific in 1804 with about fifty men to cross the new purchase. They mapped the country, sought a practical route through the mountains, and recorded its plants, animals, and peoples. Background: Jefferson had planned the expedition even before the purchase, because he wanted to know what the West held.
rationales.general:
1. Look at the image. Explorers meet Native peoples on an open plain, a century later as the painter imagined it.
2. Ask who sent them. Jefferson, who wanted to know the new territory.
3. Ask what they carried home. Maps, journals, and reports on routes, resources, and peoples.
4. Put it together. The expedition was a survey, not a conquest: knowledge first, settlement after.
Remember: an expedition's purpose is written in its orders, so ask what the explorers were told to bring back.
